subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Early Roads and Speed Laws
description: A micro-lesson that makes Early Roads and Speed Laws usable.

hook.text: When cars arrived, roads were dirt paths built for horses. Drivers had nowhere good to go.

buildup.text: Cars threw up dust clouds, scared horses, and got stuck in mud constantly.

discovery.text: Cities began paving roads with asphalt in the early 1900s, and car owners lobbied for more.

twist.text: Speed limits started absurdly low—some towns set them at 2 mph in residential areas.

climax.text: By the 1920s, paved highways connected cities and cars finally had real freedom to roam.

punchline.text: Cars didn't just need engines—they needed roads.

quiz.question: What were early roads designed for?

details.summary: The first automobiles shared rutted horse paths and faced hostile regulations like Britain's Red Flag Act, which required a person to walk ahead of any motorized vehicle waving a warning flag.
details.whyItMatters: Early road infrastructure and laws shaped how fast cars could be adopted. The push for paved roads and sensible speed limits was as important as the car itself.
takeaways: Britain's Red Flag Act limited cars to 4 mph with a flag bearer
Early roads were built for horses and completely unsuited to cars
Lobbying by motorists led to the first paved highway networks

faq.question: When were the first speed limits established?
faq.answer: Britain's Locomotive Act of 1865 set a 4 mph limit. Connecticut enacted the first US auto speed limit of 12 mph in 1901. Limits gradually increased as roads and vehicle safety improved.

faq.question: Who pushed for paved roads in America?
faq.answer: Cyclists in the Good Roads Movement of the 1890s started the push, and motorist organizations like the AAA continued the campaign. The Federal Aid Road Act of 1916 began federal highway funding.
